facts.value: The main institutions of law in industrialised countries are independent courts, representative parliaments, an accountable executive, the military and police, bureaucratic organisation, the legal profession, and civil society itself.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: John Locke, in his Two Treatises of Government, and Baron de Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws, advocated for a separation of powers between the political, legislative, and executive bodies.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Their principle was that no person should be able to usurp all powers of the state, in contrast to the absolutist theory of Thomas Hobbes' Leviathan.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Sun Yat-sen's Five Power Constitution for the Republic of China took the separation of powers further by having two additional branches of government—a Control Yuan for auditing oversight and an Examination Yuan to manage the employment of public officials.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Modern military, policing, and bureaucratic power over ordinary citizens' daily lives pose special problems for accountability that earlier writers such as Locke or Montesquieu could not have foreseen.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: The customs and practices of the legal profession are an important part of people's access to justice.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Civil society refers to the social institutions, communities, and partnerships that form the political basis of law.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA
